I am writing to provide critical feedback regarding my consultation on Friday the 20th.
During that appointment, I presented with active blisters on both my index finger and forearm. I explicitly informed the GP of my clinical history with HSV-1 and raised concerns that this new, painful presentation could be shingles or a related viral spread.
The GP confirmed the viral nature of the blisters during the examination but opted for a 'wait and see' approach, providing no medication. This was a significant diagnostic and therapeutic omission for the following reasons: The 72-Hour Window: Viral infections of this nature require immediate antiviral intervention to prevent replication. If I had waited until the following Monday for a new consultation, my condition would have deteriorated significantly. Nerve Involvement: I clearly reported forearm pain, which, combined with the blisters, pointed to herpetic involvement of the nerve (later identified as Herpetic Whitlow). Patient-Led Intervention: Due to the lack of a prescription, I was forced to self-initiate treatment using residual Aciclovir and private sourcing. My immediate action in the first 72 hours is the only reason the infection was contained. As a patient, I expect a GP to act with more vigilance when a viral infection is confirmed, especially when the patient presents with a known history and active neurological pain. However, I wanted to note that the device I am using (Hilo) is not a typical consumer wearable. It has been evaluated in multiple clinical studies and is calibrated against cuff-based measurements, effectively providing continuous, ambulatory-style monitoring rather than isolated spot readings.

In this instance, I had already supplied over 200 readings taken across different times of day, which the second GP was happy to use to inform the medication adjustment.

I thought it might be helpful to share this feedback, as these types of clinically validated continuous monitoring devices may become increasingly relevant alongside traditional cuff measurements.

I am writing to formally document my experience with Dr Adib and Dr Emiliani, which I consider to represent a significant failure in the standard of care I was entitled to receive.
Since December 2025 I have been suffering from considerable and ongoing pain resulting from foraminal stenosis, a condition further complicated by a documented history of spinal injury. Over the course of several months I made repeated attempts to obtain appropriate medical attention, including both in-person consultations and telephone appointments with the above-named practitioners. During each of these interactions I specifically and clearly requested an MRI scan, which represents a standard diagnostic measure for a condition of this nature.
Despite these repeated requests, neither Dr Adib nor Dr Emiliani took the necessary steps to investigate my condition appropriately. More concerningly, my documented history of spinal injury was entirely disregarded, despite its clear clinical relevance to my presenting symptoms. A patient’s medical history must inform clinical decision making at every stage, and the failure to account for it in this case is, in my view, indefensible.
As a direct consequence of this inaction, I was compelled to seek care elsewhere and to change my GP practice entirely, causing further delays to my treatment and adding unnecessary burden during an already difficult period.
I intend to share this account across multiple channels, as I believe the wider public has a right to be informed. I would strongly urge the relevant medical and regulatory bodies to review whether the practitioners concerned are meeting the standards of continuous professional development and patient centred care that their profession demands.

I requested blood tests because unfortunately two crucial tests had not been included in a recent blood test requested by the rheumatology clinic at C&W hospital.  Immediately agreed.  I asked if I could have 5% Fenbid gel instead of 10% Fenbid gel to help with neck/shoulder pain.  I have been waiting 29 weeks for nerve root injections (despite the referral coming from a Consultant Professor of Neurosurgery!) Immediately agreed.  There was a discussion about how to make a formal complaint to NHS West and North London.  On 05/12/25 an outstanding, fully qualified, experienced GP took my clinical history, examined me and requested an ultrasound at C&W hospital. A clinician who has never met me, never taken my clinical history nor examined me cancelled the ultrasound because “it did not conform to the guidelines”.  NHS W&NL took 9 weeks to inform the Good Practice.  What has been achieved?  Did my pain go away?  No. The GP/Patient relationship could have been seriously undermined.  I am most fortunate that I am a patient of the Good Practice.  In December I had 4 appointments in 12 days.  The GP responsible was absolutely determined to help me and I am pleased to say that I am making good progress.  However, I am aware that my experience probably wouldn’t be the experience of other patients at other practices.  A patient goes to their GP.  The GP refers them for an ultrasound.  The patient (patiently) waits for an appointment.  After 9 weeks the GP finds out that the referral has been cancelled.  The patient has to go back to their GP to start the process all over again.  The next time their GP says they are going to refer them to a clinic or for imaging does the patient believe the GP will be successful?  Trust the GP?  Probably not. I wish to make a complaint to NHS W&NL to make them aware that rejections like this are undermining the GP/patient relationship and that the NWL guidelines need to be revised.  I am aware that NHS resources are limited/very stretched and inappropriate/unjustified referrals would clog up the system, but GP’s and their clinical judgement should not be undermined.  GP’s are being given an ever increasing workload and should be supported.  The GP was most supportive of me making this complaint to NHS W&NL.

Subject: Formal patient feedback and concerns regarding communication practices, patient records, and professional standards

Dear Madam,

I write in my capacity as a registered patient of Kensington Park Medical Centre to raise formal concerns regarding interactions with the practice. This correspondence is submitted in accordance with the practice’s feedback procedure and the NHS Constitution for England. It is intended as constructive feedback directed solely at the specific issues outlined below and does not seek to impugn the wider body of clinical or administrative staff.

1. Communication preferences and threats concerning email or written correspondence

I have been advised or threatened against sending emails or maintaining written records of interactions. Under the General Medical Council’s Good Medical Practice (2024), Domain 2 (Patients, partnership and communication), registered medical practitioners must treat patients with kindness, courtesy and respect; listen to patients and acknowledge their concerns and knowledge of their own health; and communicate in a manner that supports shared decision-making. The NHS Constitution affirms the right of patients to receive information in a form they can understand and to be involved in decisions about their care.
While practices retain operational discretion over preferred channels, an absolute prohibition or threat in response to a patient’s request for written communication risks undermining the partnership principle and may engage the duty to make reasonable adjustments under the Equality Act 2010 where a patient’s health condition substantially and long-term adversely affects their ability to articulate matters verbally.

2. Audio recording of consultations with patient consent

Patients in the United Kingdom are generally entitled to make audio recordings of consultations in which they participate for purely personal use. Such recordings fall outside the scope of the UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018 when made for domestic/personal purposes (Article 2(2)(c) UK GDPR). Guidance from the British Medical Association and commentary in the medical literature confirm that clinicians should not refuse to proceed with a consultation solely because a patient wishes to record it for personal reference. Open discussion and mutual transparency are encouraged as a matter of professional courtesy and trust.
Accurate contemporaneous records, including those generated by patients, support patient safety and may assist in the prevention of incomplete or inaccurate entries that could contribute to diagnostic errors. The World Health Organization’s Patient Safety Rights Charter (2024) emphasizes the rights to information, access to medical records, and patient engagement. Principles articulated by the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights regarding the right to the highest attainable standard of health further underscore the importance of transparent information exchange.

3. Consideration of written health information provided by the patient

Where a patient has formally documented and submitted relevant health information in writing because of difficulties in verbal articulation arising from illness, the failure to acknowledge, consider, or respond to that information in a clinically appropriate manner may fall short of the standards in Good Medical Practice requiring doctors to take account of patients’ concerns and to work in partnership. The NHS Constitution and NICE guidance on patient experience reinforce the expectation that information will be provided and received in accessible formats.

4. Threats of removal from the practice list

The General Medical Council’s guidance Ending your professional relationship with a patient states that a relationship should only be ended in rare circumstances. A patient must not be removed solely because they have made a complaint. In adherence to legal mandates, the contractual clauses of the National Health Service (General Medical Services Contracts) align with the aforementioned recommendations.
Threats of removal in response to a patient’s request for written communication or the exercise of the right to record for personal use would, if substantiated, raise serious questions under the above framework and under the Human Rights Act 1998 (Articles 2, 8 and 14, read with the Equality Act 2010 where disability is engaged).

5. Professional standards and accountability

I note that I hold professional qualifications myself. Adverse treatment is not justified solely by a patient's polite and professional disagreement or their expression of a reasoned clinical opinion, particularly when the patient is a qualified professional. Any such response would risk inconsistency with the GMC’s requirements of fairness, respect, and the avoidance of discrimination.
I acknowledge with appreciation the service provided by those members of the clinical and administrative team who continue to discharge their duties in accordance with professional standards and who are not implicated in the matters raised.
